records.text: What changed: a single piece now sits where it touches several targets at once. It follows that one reply is unlikely to cover all of them.
One detail is different after this move: an enemy piece can now reach a square from which several targets are hit together.
The stronger move would have set one piece against several targets. After this move, that arrangement never appears.
A piece now stands on the line between its king and an attacker. Stepping off that line is no longer a legal option for it.
The piece in front of the king has become pinnable. Once the pin arrives, leaving that line stops being legal.
With the stronger move, an enemy piece would have been fixed in front of its king. As it is, that piece keeps every option.
The front piece on the line is under attack now. When it steps away, what was standing behind it becomes the target.
After this move, two pieces are lined up so the other side can skewer them. The front one would have to step away, leaving the rear one exposed.
A skewer sat inside the stronger move: pressure on the front piece, the real target behind it. After this move the line remains untouched.
The piece doing the defending has been captured. Whatever depended on it has lost that cover.
A defender has become capturable. If it is taken, the piece it was covering no longer has that support.
The stronger move would have captured a defender and stripped cover from what it guarded. That defender is still standing.
The king's exits are occupied by its own pieces, and its last rank has become the point of attack.
After this move the king has no square off its back rank, and a mate along that rank is available to the other side.
The enemy king had no way off its back rank; its own pieces were in the way. The mate that this allowed was not played.
The pawn has moved a step nearer promotion. It follows that the defense has fewer moves in hand.
A route toward promotion has opened for an enemy pawn. Each further step it takes will require an answer.
The stronger move would have carried a pawn closer to its promotion square. In this position that pawn is where it was.
The front piece has stepped off the line, and the piece that was behind it now attacks along it.
One enemy piece now screens another. Once the screening piece moves, the one behind it attacks down the opened line.
The stronger move would have uncovered an attack by moving a front piece off its line. That line has stayed shut.
One move, and now there are threats in two places. It follows that a single reply rarely deals with both.
After this move, the other side could create two threats with a single move.
The stronger move would have produced two threats together. No such pair arises from this one.
The defender has been drawn away from its job, and what it was covering is uncovered now.
One defender can now be lured away from what it was covering.
The stronger move would have drawn a defender off its job. Here the defender has not been disturbed.
The piece that was captured had no defender, so there is no recapture available.
With the stronger move, an enemy piece without protection could have been taken. It is still standing.
After this move one piece has lost all of its protection, and the other side can take it with nothing coming back.
This piece was the only real defender of another. It has gone elsewhere, so the piece it guarded is now open to capture.
A threat appeared with the opponent's last move. This reply leaves the threat as it was, so a piece is still capturable.
The exchange has a second half. The recapture removes a more valuable piece, so the material count falls overall.
One minor piece is no longer at home; it has been brought into play.
With the alternative, a minor piece would have been developed. Here that piece is still at home.
The rook's file no longer holds a pawn of either color.
The alternative would have put a rook on a file free of pawns of both colors.
The rook's file has changed character: no pawn of its own color remains on it, while an enemy pawn does. That makes it semi-open.
The alternative would have placed a rook where none of its own pawns block the file and enemy pawns still stand.
A pawn has become passed. Neither on its file nor on the two beside it is there an enemy pawn ahead.
The alternative would have given a pawn a clear path, with no enemy pawn ahead on its own file or on either side.
The passed pawn stands a square further on than before.
The alternative pushed the passed pawn on. Here it keeps its square.
A pawn has become isolated: neither neighboring file holds a pawn of its color any longer.
The alternative would have isolated a pawn, leaving both neighboring files without a pawn of its color.
Before this move, a piece had no defender. Now it has one.
The alternative would have supplied a defender to a piece that has none at the moment.
A piece has lost its last defender. The weakness is real; it does not on its own show the piece can be won.
The alternative would have taken away a piece's last defender. By itself, that would not have shown it could be won.
The king has one more legal square than before. Something on the board changed to make that room.
The alternative would have given the king one additional legal square.
The king has castled. It moved two squares, and the rook has crossed to its other side.
Castling was available, moving king and rook together in a single turn.
Before this capture there was a bishop pair; now there is not. That side's remaining bishop covers only one square color.
With the alternative, a bishop would have been captured and the opposing pair would have ended.
Before this move the pawns stood on different files; now two of the same color share one. They are doubled.
The alternative would have left two pawns doubled up on a single file.
Something decisive has shifted. From here a forced checkmate is in the other side's hands, and the reason lies in the moves before this one.
The mating line that existed before this move no longer exists after it. A forced checkmate went unplayed.
Material has been offered. The checked line shows the idea survives even if the offer is accepted.
Among the examined moves, only this one keeps the position playable. Every other one loses.
Among the examined moves, this is the one that keeps the advantage. All the others lose.
The first change to note: on its next move, the other side has a capture available.
The strongest reply arrives as a check. The king's safety now comes before anything else.
What the engine would play here is something different. After the strongest reply, the two lines go different ways.
Compared with the engine's top move, part of the value is gone. Follow the reply to see where the gap opens.
Strong. Compared with the engine's choices, very little value has changed hands.
Sound. The engine leans toward another move, yet most of the position's value is still in place.
As the human-move model sees it, this move is the natural one. The engine prefers another, and the reply shows what the difference costs.
As the human-move model sees it, few would play this, and yet the engine rates it as strong. Both observations stand side by side.
A single move would have held the position here, and by the human-move model's reading that defense was hard to find.
Both the human-move model and the searched alternatives point the same way: this was hard to find. It was found all the same.
The position still holds. By the human-move model and the searched alternatives, the defense was a hard one, and it was found.
By the human-move model's reading this is the expected move, and the engine places nothing above it. On this one, the two measures agree.
As the human-move model sees it, this move is the natural one. The engine rates it strong and would pick a different one.
The clock had almost run down by the time this move was chosen.
This move came quickly; most of the clock was still unused.
A good deal of clock time was used before this move.
This move is one a recognized opening contains.
The game moves outside the known opening at this point. From here, the position is unfamiliar.
After the earlier error, the position has become playable again. That is the change worth recording.
The earlier error has stopped being decisive, and the game is playable once more. The other side's mistakes played a part in that.
The opponent's last move left something available. This move collects it.
The opponent's last move left something available. This reply does not take it, and a stronger answer existed.
This issue is not new in this game; it came up once already. Placed side by side, the two moments share a pattern.
A piece lost its protection earlier on. That protection has returned.
Small concessions keep accumulating, and this move is another of them. One by one they are minor; together they have shifted the position.
From that point until the recorded win, the advantage stayed in place and was never handed back.
This issue is not limited to this game; other saved games contain it as well. The positions share a common thread.
Checkmate. No legal move remains for the king, and the game has ended.
Checkmate. Every legal move is gone for the defending king. The decisions leading here are where things changed.
A draw. The result is fixed, though the decisions along the way remain worth examining.
Look at the position as it stands, then choose a move.
Not the answer. Look again at what the last move changed.
The attempt went through without a result. Enter the move once again.
According to the saved engine analysis, a forced checkmate is now in the hands of the side that played this move.
The saved engine analysis records that this move leaves its own side facing a forced checkmate.
Set the material at the end of the saved line beside the material at its start: the side that played this move has gained.
Set the material at the end of the saved line beside the material at its start: the side that played this move has lost some.
This move is accepted. Nothing in the moves shown gives a clear tactical reason, and none is supposed.
The exercise does not take this move, and nothing in the moves shown points to a clear tactical reason. Look over what changed once more.
It appears among the saved answers, which are the standard in this exercise.
None of the saved answers is this move. That does not rule it out as sound chess.
Take note of the move and its reason, and continue with the next position.
Correct. What transfers to other positions is the reason, more than the move itself.
The practice has been recorded, and the review schedule is the same as before.
Solved. For now, this recall stays marked as relearning.
This is how the position looked before any of these moves.
One move is played. Note what is different afterward.
Check. Until it is answered, nothing else matters.
The check has been answered; the king is clear.
The pawn has reached the last rank and been replaced by a new piece.
After the promotion, the new piece is giving check.
After the promotion, the position is checkmate.
After the promotion, its own king is out of check as well.
A capture. There is one piece fewer on the board.
After the capture, the king is in check.
After the capture, the position is checkmate.
After the capture, the king is out of check.
With a capture, the pawn arrives on the last rank and is replaced by a new piece.
After capturing and promoting, the new piece is giving check.
After capturing and promoting, the position is checkmate.
After capturing and promoting, its own king is out of check.
After castling, the opposing king is in check.
After castling, the position is checkmate.
A fork in operation: one piece threatens several targets and, a little later, captures one. By the end of this example there is a net material gain.
The marked capture is not legal here. This piece is pinned, and moving it would expose its king.
Pinned to its king, the attacked piece only has moves that keep that king shielded.
No recapture comes, because each defender is pinned to its king. That is why the capture is possible, and the line shown ends with more material.
The pinned piece cannot leave its line while its king stands behind. Before the sequence ends, it is captured.
Once the front piece steps off the line, the one that stood behind it is captured.
A check sends the king off the line, and the same attacker then captures what was behind it.
The lone defender is captured, and after it, the piece it was protecting.
The defender is drawn away from where it stood, and what it was covering is captured next.
The blocking piece steps off the line; the piece behind it then captures along the opening it left.
One piece leaves the line, and check comes through the gap it left.
Double check. With two pieces giving check, only a king move is possible.
Two targets, two attackers: the moving piece threatens one, and the line it opened threatens the other. The piece behind collects.
Promotion. When this example finishes, that side is also ahead on material.
A piece without protection is taken, and the capturing side finishes this example with more material.
A relative pin had been holding the attacking piece. The opponent's previous move lifted it, and the piece captures a target that never moved, in the line shown.
The other side is permitted the marked reply. Play it on the board and note what changes.
Before moving, check that no piece is left to be taken without a recapture.
Before a quiet move, check whether any enemy piece has lost its protection.
Among the forcing moves, notice whether one piece could land on two valuable targets.
Before a pinned piece moves, consider what it shields, whether that is the king or a piece of greater value.
Note what stands behind the first target. A more valuable piece may be on the same line.
Before a defender is traded, note what it is protecting.
When a piece moves off a line, note what that line now reaches.
Note any single move that creates two threats, including checks and lines it opens.
If a back-rank defender is about to move, first confirm the king will still have an escape square.
Note how many squares a pawn still needs to promote, and which of its moves demand a reply.
Before a defender moves, note which pieces rely on it.
Before capturing, weigh what is won against what the recapture would remove.
Note whether a forcing exchange could draw a defender away from a second task.
Here the saved answers are the measure. Outside them, a legal move may still be sound.
The line uses strong replies. Those are not the only ones possible.
Within the line shown, material is counted from that line's own first position. The written explanation gives the values used for each piece.
No simple tactical reason can be read from the saved line, and no positional one is supposed. Play it out and note how each reply changes things.
The answer policy stored with this exercise determines how it is explained, and its setting is written in the notes.
Here is the opening line, each move in order.
Correct. That move belongs to your study material.
Choose a move from the opening lines you are studying.
This position appears in more than one of your chosen opening lines, and each of them offers a valid move.
Recall the move that comes next in your study material.
That move does not appear in your chosen opening lines. Try again.
That is outside your chosen lines; try again. The study was edited, so review dates are unaffected by this saved attempt.
That is outside your chosen lines; try again. The position is retired, so its review dates do not change.
Any move from this line is accepted under Mixed Due. Dedicated practice wants this specific line and no other.
Due recalls will ask for the moves of your chosen side. Where several active studies share a position, there is one card for it.
Another move needs the saved session reloaded first.
The verified line is now being played out on the board.
The record lists this attempt as revealed. The solution is still below.
Solved, after an earlier miss. The record keeps that miss as well.
Solved, and no wrong move along the way.
This puzzle asks for a different move. Moves already played correctly are still saved.
Correct. The puzzle continues with the next move.
Observe the position carefully, and move once the line is clear.
There is not enough engine analysis to explain this position, so no explanation is given.
Review paused. It continues below, or a move can be tried on the board.
Pick any move to revisit, or play one of your own on the board.
With this move, the game has entered a recognized opening.
The game stays on mapped ground; a known opening already has this move on file.
There is an entry for this move in the opening book.
Still no departure from the book.
This one is in the book too.
Even the reply sticks to the book.
The book line carries on unchanged.
One more move that the book contains.
Nothing has left the book yet.
Once more, a book move.
Still the book. That places the game; it says nothing about the move's quality.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one. What it changes is decisive: a forced checkmate now belongs to the other side, and the cause sits in the defense before this point.
A forced checkmate existed before this move and is gone after it. The human-move model counts the move routine; when the enemy king is exposed, checks deserve the first look.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, yet after it something can be captured at once. That reply is the first thing that changed.
An ordinary-looking move by the human-move model's reading. The engine prefers another, and following the reply shows the value that went missing.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but it lets an enemy piece land on a square that hits several targets. That piece is the thing to locate.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but it leaves two pieces lined up for the other side to skewer, front one driven off and rear one exposed.
Every other searched move loses, and this one alone leaves the position playable. In the human-move model's reading that defense was hard to find, and it was found.

This is the move that leaves the game playable; the rest of the examined moves lose. Top of the engine's ranking, this move is also one the human-move model and the searched alternatives single out as hard to find.
Only through this move does the advantage remain; every alternative examined loses. In the human-move model's reading the resource was difficult, and it was found.
The advantage stays only through this move; the other examined options all lose. Hard to find in the human-move model's reading and best in the engine's, and it was found.
A fork has appeared, one piece now facing several targets. This move falls outside the human-move model's predictions, which does not change the engine's view that it is strong.
A fork that was not easy to see, one piece now facing several targets. The human-move model puts this move's chance of being found low, and the engine places it at the top.
A piece is now pinned to its king and can no longer legally step off its line. By the human-move model's reading this move is unlikely, and by the engine's reading it is strong, so the two differ.
A pin against the king now holds a piece where it stands. Best in the engine's search and difficult in the human-move model's reading, this move was located.
An ordinary-looking move by the human-move model's reading. But this piece was the only real defender of another, and that other piece has become capturable.

The only defender has gone elsewhere, and what it was guarding is now capturable. Of the searched moves, just one would have held, and that defense ranks as hard to find in the human-move model's reading.
The threat from the opponent's last move is still there after this reply, a routine one in the human-move model's terms. A piece remains capturable.
Nothing about the opponent's threat has changed, and a piece is still capturable. The defense that held was a different move, one the human-move model marks as difficult.
To the human-move model the capture looks natural. The recapture then removes something more valuable, so the material count drops.
This capture is answered by a recapture of higher value, and the count drops. There was exactly one searched move that kept the position, and the human-move model classes it as difficult to see.
A fork: one piece now stands against several targets. Set the human-move model's prediction beside the engine's ranking and no difference appears; this move is both the natural one and the best.
After this move, several targets are under attack from one piece. Observed by the human-move model as natural and by the engine as strong, this move is still not the engine's first preference.
The other side has gained access to a fork. One particular defense was needed here, and the human-move model expects few players to locate it.
A fork was part of the stronger move. With this one, rated natural by the human-move model, the position has none.
The holding defense came with a fork, yet this move passes it by. Few players would find it, in the human-move model's reading.
A pin: the piece in front of the king has lost the right to leave its line. The human-move model would have predicted this move, and the engine's search turns up nothing that improves on it.
A piece in front of its king is pinned there now. By the human-move model's reading it is natural, and by the engine's it is strong, with the engine leaning toward another move.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but a piece in front of its king can now be pinned, after which it could no longer leave the line.
After this move, the other side can pin a piece against its king. A single searched move would have held, and in the human-move model's reading few would have found it.
With the stronger move, an enemy piece would have been fixed to its king. With this one, rated natural by the human-move model, it keeps its freedom.
A pin against the king was the holding defense, yet this move passes it by. That defense counts as rare in the human-move model's reading.

A skewer: the front piece is attacked, and once it moves, what was behind it is exposed. The searched alternatives and the human-move model both mark this move as hard to see, and the engine ranks it highest.
An unexpected skewer; the front piece now has to leave its line. The human-move model gives this move a low probability, and still the engine's search supports it as strong.

The front piece on the line has to give way, and what stood behind it becomes exposed. No gap opens between the two measures here, since the move the human-move model expects is the move the engine puts first.
A skewer now runs along one line. The human-move model has this move in its forecast, while the engine rates it strong and would have chosen a different one.
Two pieces now stand on one line where the other side can skewer them. The move that would have held lay elsewhere, and the human-move model scores its chance of being found as low.
There was a skewer in the stronger move. This one, rated natural by the human-move model, leaves that line as it was.
The holding defense used a skewer, yet this move passes it by. That defense counts as rare in the human-move model's reading.
A defender has been captured, and with it the cover it gave. A move the human-move model considers difficult to find turns out to be the engine's top choice.
The capture removes a defender, so the piece it covered is now exposed. Few players would pick it, according to the human-move model, while the engine sees it as strong.
With its defender gone, the protected piece now stands alone. Here the obvious move and the strongest move are the same one, as the human-move model and the engine each report.
One defender is no longer on the board. The two readings sit slightly apart here, natural for the human-move model and strong but not preferred for the engine.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but a defender has become capturable, and the piece it covers would lose that cover.
A defender has become available for capture. Of the searched moves, just one would have held, and that defense ranks as hard to find in the human-move model's reading.
With the stronger move, a defender would have come off the board. With this one, rated natural by the human-move model, it stays on duty.
The holding defense captured a defender, yet this move passes it by. In the human-move model's reading, few would locate it.
On the back rank, the king's own pieces now cover every exit. The engine prefers this move to every alternative, though the human-move model rates it difficult to locate.
The king is confined to its last rank, and that rank has become the target. Marked unusual by the human-move model and strong by the engine, this move sits where the two readings diverge.
The back rank is now the weak point; the king has no way off it. The human-move model's expectation and the engine's first choice land on the same move in this position.
A mating pattern has formed on the back rank. To the human-move model this is the natural move, and the engine accepts it as strong while favoring something else.
The pawn is a step nearer promotion, and the defense has fewer moves in hand. At the top of the engine's list and hard to find by the human-move model's measure, this move was located anyway.
A pawn has begun to move toward the last rank. This move lies outside what the human-move model expects, and inside what the engine considers strong.
The pawn now stands nearer its promotion square. Nothing in the engine's search ranks above this move, and the human-move model had already marked it as natural.
A pawn moves on toward its promotion square. Natural in the human-move model's estimate and strong in the engine's, though the engine's first choice lies elsewhere.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but an enemy pawn's route to promotion has opened wider.
After this move, an enemy pawn has a route toward promotion. The defense that held was a different move, one the human-move model marks as difficult.
With the stronger move, a pawn would have gone toward promotion. With this one, rated natural by the human-move model, the pawn has not moved.
A pawn push toward promotion was the holding defense, yet this move passes it by. Few players would find it, in the human-move model's reading.
Its front piece has stepped aside, so the line behind is open and attacking. The human-move model would not expect most players to find this move, and the engine ranks it best.
An unexpected move has uncovered an attack along a line. The human-move model scores this move as improbable, while the engine places it among the strong ones.
The line is open now, and the piece that was behind attacks along it. Both readings settle in the same place, with the human-move model calling it natural and the engine placing it on top.
Moving the front piece has uncovered an attack. The human-move model would forecast this move, and the engine rates it strong while keeping a different move as its own pick.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but the other side can now uncover an attack by moving a front piece.
After this move, the other side can uncover an attack along a line. There was exactly one searched move that kept the position, and the human-move model classes it as difficult to see.
With the stronger move, an attack would have been uncovered. With this one, rated natural by the human-move model, the line stays shut.
A discovered attack was part of the defense that would have held, yet this move passes it by. Few players would see it, in the human-move model's reading.
This move has produced threats in two places. Difficult in the human-move model's reading and top of the engine's ranking, this one was located.
An unexpected move, and two threats now stand at once. The human-move model would not have forecast this, yet the engine's evaluation of it holds up as strong.
Two targets are threatened now, and both by one move. This is the move the human-move model anticipates and also the one the engine ranks highest, so the two readings coincide.
Two threats now stand, and each will need its own reply. Natural, on the human-move model's measure, and strong, as the engine measures it, although the engine still points to another move.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but the other side now has a single move that would create two threats.
A move that makes two threats at once is now open to the other side. One particular defense was needed here, and the human-move model expects few players to locate it.
The stronger move produced two threats together. This one, which the human-move model treats as ordinary, produces no such pair.
The holding defense produced two threats at once, yet this move passes it by. That defense counts as rare in the human-move model's reading.
A deflection: the defender has abandoned its task. Top of the engine's ranking, this move is also one the human-move model and the searched alternatives single out as hard to find.
An unexpected move has drawn the defender away. Unexpected for the human-move model and strong for the engine, two observations that both stand.
The defender has been pulled off, and what it covered is now uncovered. The human-move model rates it natural, and when the engine compares the alternatives, none of them comes out ahead.
A defender has been deflected from its job. The human-move model sees nothing unusual in this move, and the engine rates it strong while choosing differently itself.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but a defender can now be lured away from what it covers.
After this move, a defender can be drawn off its task. A single searched move would have held, and in the human-move model's reading few would have found it.
With the stronger move, a defender would have been pulled off its task. With this one, rated natural by the human-move model, it has not moved.
The holding defense deflected a defender, yet this move passes it by. Few players would find it, in the human-move model's reading.
A piece with no protection has been taken. Hard to find in the human-move model's reading and best in the engine's, and it was found.
An undefended piece is gone, collected by an unexpected route. The human-move model rates this move unlikely while the engine rates it strong, a gap worth noting.
Nothing defended that piece, and now it is off the board. Predicted by the human-move model and unmatched in the engine's search, this move shows no difference between the two.
One undefended piece has been captured. Routine for the human-move model, strong for the engine, and still not the engine's own choice.
The stronger move captured an unprotected piece. With this one, which the human-move model treats as ordinary, that piece is still standing.
Capturing an unprotected piece was the holding defense, yet this move passes it by. In the human-move model's reading, few would locate it.
In the human-move model's terms the move is a routine one, but one piece has lost all protection, and the other side can take it.
After this move, one piece has no protection left. The move that would have held lay elsewhere, and the human-move model scores its chance of being found as low.
A minor piece has come into play. The human-move model puts this move's chance of being found low, and the engine places it at the top. A quiet move can be the hardest kind to find.
An unexpected way to bring a minor piece into play. This move falls outside the human-move model's predictions, which does not change the engine's view that it is strong.
A minor piece is out and in play now. Set the human-move model's prediction beside the engine's ranking and no difference appears; this move is both the natural one and the best.
Another minor piece is now part of the game. Observed by the human-move model as natural and by the engine as strong, this move is still not the engine's first preference.
There are no pawns on the rook's new file. Best in the engine's search and difficult in the human-move model's reading, this move was located.
By an unexpected route, the rook has reached an open file. By the human-move model's reading this move is unlikely, and by the engine's reading it is strong, so the two differ.
The rook's file is clear of pawns now. The human-move model would have predicted this move, and the engine's search turns up nothing that improves on it.
With this move, the rook has an open file. By the human-move model's reading it is natural, and by the engine's it is strong, with the engine leaning toward another move.
Only enemy pawns now stand on the rook's file. The searched alternatives and the human-move model both mark this move as hard to see, and the engine ranks it highest.
An unexpected route has brought the rook to a semi-open file. The human-move model gives this move a low probability, and still the engine's search supports it as strong.
Of the pawns on the rook's file, none are its own anymore. No gap opens between the two measures here, since the move the human-move model expects is the move the engine puts first.
With this move, the rook has a semi-open file. The human-move model has this move in its forecast, while the engine rates it strong and would have chosen a different one.
A pawn has become passed: on its file and both neighbors, nothing of the enemy's stands ahead. A move the human-move model considers difficult to find turns out to be the engine's top choice.
An unexpected move has produced a passed pawn. Few players would pick it, according to the human-move model, while the engine sees it as strong.
One of the pawns is now a passed pawn. Here the obvious move and the strongest move are the same one, as the human-move model and the engine each report.
With this move, one pawn is passed. The two readings sit slightly apart here, natural for the human-move model and strong but not preferred for the engine.
The passed pawn has moved up one square. The engine prefers this move to every alternative, though the human-move model rates it difficult to locate.
An unexpected advance by the passed pawn. Marked unusual by the human-move model and strong by the engine, this move sits where the two readings diverge.
The passed pawn stands a square further on. The human-move model's expectation and the engine's first choice land on the same move in this position.
